marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q019.takeaway: Seminal vesicles contribute most of semen volume, supplying fructose-rich alkaline secretion.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q019.displayText:
Seminal vesicles contribute most of semen volume, supplying fructose-rich alkaline secretion.

The major contribution to semen is from seminal vesicles.

The seminal vesicles contribute ~60-70% of the volume of semen. Apart from sperm, the remaining 20-40% represents epididymal fluids, as well as secretion of the prostate gland and bulbourethral glands.

The seminal plasma originates primarily from the accessory glands (the seminal vesicles, the prostate gland, and the bulbourethral glands).
emphasis: Seminal vesicles contribute most of semen volume, supplying fructose-rich alkaline secretion

rationales.b: Cowper glands contribute a small lubricating pre-ejaculate volume.
rationales.c: Prostate contributes a substantial but smaller fraction than seminal vesicles.
rationales.d: Urethral glands add only a minor mucous secretion.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q020.takeaway: Normal semen is mildly alkaline, with pH around 7.4 to support sperm survival.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q020.displayText:
Normal semen is mildly alkaline, with pH around 7.4 to support sperm survival.

The normal pH of human semen is 7.4 (isotonic).

The pH in the lumen of the epididymis is relatively acidic (6.5 to 6.8) as the result of H+ secretion by clear cells that are analogous to intercalated cells in the nephron. Addition of the relatively alkaline secretions of the seminal vesicles raises the final pH of seminal plasma to between 7.2 and 7.8.

Spermatozoa generally tolerate alkalinity better than acidity.

A pH near neutrality or slightly higher is optimal for the motility and survival of sperm cells in humans and in other species as well.
emphasis: Normal semen is mildly alkaline, with pH around 7

rationales.a: pH 7 is neutral rather than the usual mildly alkaline semen value.
rationales.b: pH 6.5 is acidic and can impair sperm survival.
rationales.d: pH 8 is more alkaline than the standard value in this item.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q021.takeaway: Seminal vesicles secrete much of the prostaglandin content of semen.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q021.displayText:
Seminal vesicles secrete much of the prostaglandin content of semen.

Prostaglandins in semen are secreted by seminal vesicle.

The seminal vesicles secrete fluid that is rich in fructose, citrate, prostaglandins, and fibrinogen.

The prostaglandins present in the seminal fluid may assist in fertilization in two ways:
• Prostaglandins react with cervical mucus to make it more penetrable by sperm.
• Prostaglandins induce peristaltic contractions in the female reproductive tract (i.e., the uterus and fallopian tubes) to propel the sperm up the tract.
emphasis: Seminal vesicles secrete much of the prostaglandin content of semen

rationales.b: Cowper glands mainly secrete lubricating mucus.
rationales.c: The prostate contributes citrate, enzymes and fluid, but seminal vesicles are the principal prostaglandin source.
rationales.d: Urethral glands add mucus, not the major prostaglandin component.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q022.takeaway: The source’s conventional normal sperm concentration range is about 90–120 million/mL.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q022.displayText:
The source’s conventional normal sperm concentration range is about 90–120 million/mL.

Normal sperm count on an average is 100 million/ml (90-120 million/mL).

Note: The WHO 2010 minimal criteria for semen analysis requires a minimum sperm count >15 million/mL or >40 million/per ejaculate.
emphasis: The source’s conventional normal sperm concentration range is about 90–120 million/mL

rationales.a: 20–40 million/mL is below the traditional range used by this source.
rationales.b: 40–60 million/mL is below the stated conventional normal estimate.
rationales.c: 60–80 million/mL remains below the source’s selected range.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q023.takeaway: Fertilization most commonly occurs in the ampulla, the widest segment of the uterine tube.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q023.displayText:
Fertilization most commonly occurs in the ampulla, the widest segment of the uterine tube.

In humans, fertilization of the ovum by the sperm usually occurs in the ampulla of the fallopian tube.
emphasis: Fertilization most commonly occurs in the ampulla, the widest segment of the uterine tube

rationales.a: The interstitial segment traverses the uterine wall and is not the usual fertilization site.
rationales.b: The isthmus is narrower and more medial than the usual ampullary site.
rationales.c: Fimbriae capture the ovulated oocyte but fertilization usually occurs in the ampulla.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q024.takeaway: Sperm can remain capable of fertilization in the female tract for about 24–48 hours under favorable conditions.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q024.displayText:
Sperm can remain capable of fertilization in the female tract for about 24–48 hours under favorable conditions.

After ejaculation, sperms have a maximal lifespan of 24-48 hours in the female genital tract.

The activity and rate of metabolism of sperm increase markedly with increasing temperature causing its life to be considerably shortened.

Sperm can be cryopreserved for years if agents such as glycerol are used to prevent ice crystal formation during freezing.

Note: The ovum stays viable and capable of being fertilized, probably no longer than 24 hours after it is expelled from the ovary.
emphasis: Sperm can remain capable of fertilization in the female tract for about 24–48 hours under favorable conditions

rationales.a: 6–8 hours is shorter than the typical survival window.
rationales.b: 12–24 hours can occur but understates the conventional 24–48-hour interval.
rationales.d: 72–96 hours exceeds the source’s expected fertile duration.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q025.takeaway: The ovum remains fertilizable for approximately 24 hours after ovulation.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q025.displayText:
The ovum remains fertilizable for approximately 24 hours after ovulation.

The ovum remains viable up to 24 hours following ovulation.

If not fertilized, the ovum degenerates in the fallopian tube without leaving behind any trace after 24 hours.
emphasis: The ovum remains fertilizable for approximately 24 hours after ovulation

rationales.a: 12 hours is shorter than the usual viability interval.
rationales.c: 48 hours overestimates the ovum’s short postovulatory viability.
rationales.d: 72 hours greatly exceeds the fertilizable window.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q026.takeaway: Insulin is not considered a permissive hormone required for pubertal attainment in the way GH, leptin and sex steroids are.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q026.displayText:
Insulin is not considered a permissive hormone required for pubertal attainment in the way GH, leptin and sex steroids are.

Insulin has no role in the attainment of puberty. GH, leptin and testosterone are all required for the onset of puberty.

The onset of puberty is marked by enhanced androgenic activity. The growth spurt of adolescent males is influenced by a complex interplay between androgens, growth hormone (GH), nutrition, and genetic factors.

Leptin, the satiety-producing hormone secreted by fat cells, may be the link between body weight and puberty.
emphasis: Insulin is not considered a permissive hormone required for pubertal attainment in the way GH, leptin and sex steroids are

rationales.a: GH supports normal growth and maturation during puberty.
rationales.b: Leptin signals energy sufficiency and has a permissive role in reproductive maturation.
rationales.c: Testosterone is a principal sex steroid supporting male pubertal development.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q027.takeaway: Adrenal and gonadal androgens, including testosterone, drive pubarche and axillary hair development.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q027.displayText:
Adrenal and gonadal androgens, including testosterone, drive pubarche and axillary hair development.

Pubarche or the development of axillary and pubic hair is due to testosterone.

The growth of pubic and axillary hair in both sexes is primarily due to androgens.
emphasis: Adrenal and gonadal androgens, including testosterone, drive pubarche and axillary hair development

rationales.a: GH supports growth but does not directly cause pubic hair development.
rationales.b: Progesterone is not the principal androgenic signal for pubarche.
rationales.d: Estrogen drives breast development and other female changes, not androgenic pubarche.

marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q028.takeaway: Leptin signals adequate energy stores and acts permissively on the hypothalamic reproductive axis at puberty.
marrow__PHYSIO_CH41_Q028.displayText:
Leptin signals adequate energy stores and acts permissively on the hypothalamic reproductive axis at puberty.

The hormone that plays a permissive role in the attainment of puberty is leptin.

It now appears that leptin may be the link between body weight and puberty. Leptin is a satiety-producing hormone secreted by adipocytes. High leptin levels reduce appetite and increase energy expenditure.

Evidence for which is given by:
• Obese ob/ob mice that cannot make leptin are infertile, and their fertility is restored by injections of leptin.
• Leptin treatment also induces precocious puberty in immature female mice.
• However, the way that leptin fits into the overall control of puberty remains to be determined.

Leptin also accelerates GnRH pulsatility in neurons, hastening puberty.
emphasis: Leptin signals adequate energy stores and acts permissively on the hypothalamic reproductive axis at puberty

rationales.a: GnRH is the central driver of pituitary gonadotropin release, rather than a permissive metabolic signal.
rationales.c: Insulin reflects energy status but leptin is the classic permissive adiposity signal asked.
rationales.d: GH supports growth, but leptin is the key permissive puberty signal in this option set.
